projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Mary Cummings Jongeward was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Olivia L. Olson
sp.p: Okay, today is the 10th of January and it's 2007, and my name is Olivia Olsen, and I am here to interview Mary Jongeward. And she's going to talk to us about her experiences during her service in World War II and Korea. Mary, why don't you tell us what branch of service you belonged to?

sp.speaker: Mary Cummings Jongeward
sp.p: I was in the Y Branch of the army.

sp.speaker: Olivia L. Olson
sp.p: Wonderful, and can you tell me when you entered the service?

sp.speaker: Mary Cummings Jongeward
sp.p: March 1943.

sp.speaker: Olivia L. Olson
sp.p: What was your rank while you were in the service?

sp.speaker: Mary Cummings Jongeward
sp.p: Well it's a Master Sergeant, but later -- I didn't get the Superior ____, I just got the Master Sergeant.

sp.speaker: Olivia L. Olson
sp.p: Can you tell me the reason that you joined the service?

sp.speaker: Mary Cummings Jongeward
sp.p: Well, I was -- during war times, my brother was already in the service over at Fort Sill Oklahoma. And people were conscious of the war effort, and a friend in my neighborhood said, "Mary, let's go down to Little Rock and enlist in the WAX." I said, "Well, okay, let's try it." We took the bus and went down there. I passed my physical, passed the mental, and passed everything. And then when she came out, she said -- with her papers with all X's on it -- she had TB in the active stages. So we came back, and she died about six months after that. So, I was the only one from my hometown that ever entered the women's army core, from day one until today 2007.

sp.speaker: Olivia L. Olson
sp.p: Wow. Can you tell me what some of your duties were?

sp.speaker: Mary Cummings Jongeward
sp.p: Well I was in administration. I was in the paper part of it. The army always has three copies of everything. So I was -- did various jobs. I worked in the army libraries, different libraries. Then my last assignment, I was an instructor at Fort Dix, New Jersey, and I instructed the trainees in the various military matters and the classification. Because in Germany, I had held the top secret -- no, NATO top secret, secret and confidential clearances, because I worked in security. So, when I came back to the States I taught different other subject matters, military matters, at Fort Dix, and I'd have 50 trainees in my class there at Fort Dix. It was a training center.

sp.speaker: Olivia L. Olson
sp.p: Can you tell me some of the various places that you served?

sp.speaker: Mary Cummings Jongeward
sp.p: When I joined, there were three choices. Either Fort Oglethorpe, Georgia; Daytona Beach, Florida or Fort Des Moines, Iowa. And I thought, oh it's a barge, it's cold weather, I'd like to go to either Daytona Beach or Fort Oglethorpe. When my orders came down, I was destined to go to Fort Des Moines, Iowa. I got on the train and went up there. And I had just a straight skirt, very tight, with a jacket, and when I got to the train station, they came in with a big huge army truck, and I was trying to get up that step to get in the truck. I had to pull my skirt way up, in order to get in there and I thought, well, I'm in the army now. I have to put up with this. Nobody recruited me, I am strictly on my own. I had never been away from home in my life without some of my relatives with me. That was my first time to venture out strictly on my own, and that's where I had my basic training. It was up -- you were up at six o'clock. You had 30 minutes PT or 30 minutes of drill, and they'd marched you into the mess hall after that. And my first time in the mess hall, they had a cup that was so thick, I could hardly get my lip over it to drink coffee, and huge meals. And then of course, you had all the training and marching, and then they sent you to classes. And I had all my classes there, and then when I graduated from that six weeks of basics, then they sent me into Fort Des Moines, the city of Des Moines, Iowa, where I took six more weeks of advanced training and administration. It was all administration -- that was quite interesting there. We took over all the major hotels in Des Moines, and the people, the Des Moines' people of Iowa, I think they didn't have too much use for us, because they can never get a cab, they can never get in it because the _____ were in it. Everything was taken by us at that time. And then my first assignment from there, after the basics, was at San Antonio, Texas, at the Kelly Air Force base. I was assigned to the Air Force there, and I worked there, I worked in the library and other administration duties. And I was very firm in my belief in God, and I believed in going to church every Sunday. So I had, I'd say in the barracks, there be about 40 people in the barracks, I'd say, "Anybody want to go to the chapel service?" And sometimes somebody would go, sometimes nobody would go and I would go by myself, because I never deviated in the way I was brought up. I didn't stay changing in my standards on what I wanted to do. That was my first assignment.

sp.speaker: Olivia L. Olson
sp.p: Where did you go after Kelly?

sp.speaker: Mary Cummings Jongeward
sp.p: After Kelly -- I was -- interval of time and then I got orders to report to Camp Stoneman California for duty, and they asked me -- orders came down. Would I accept assignment in the far east or in Germany, and I thought well maybe sometime in my life, maybe I'd get to go to Germany. I would take the far east. So, I had to report to Camp Stoneman California. We had bed _____ duties, carrying a pack across the desert, and different things we had to do there, in order to prepare ourself for duty in Japan. And we got on the boat -- and the ship -- and stopped at Hawaii for one day. Then on into Inchon Harbor, Korea, where they disembarked about 1500 men from the ship, there at Inchon, and then on across to Yokoyama. The ship pulled in there and then they took -- buses led us there, took us about 19 miles to Tokyo, and that's where we were belted. And of course, the ruins of Tokyo was very prevalent. There you can see bellies torn down. They hadn't rebelled or anything.

sp.speaker: Olivia L. Olson
sp.p: About what year was that?

sp.speaker: Mary Cummings Jongeward
sp.p: That was 1946, and then we were in the occupying armies. We were occupying Japan and I was part of the occupy. And I was in Douglas McArthur's headquarters, and my paperwork said by order of Douglas McArthur, and I was there working there in engineer intelligences. I was working in intelligence in there, in Tokyo. And then of course, everything, most places were off limits, and I didn't have any desire to go to the off limit places, because I was afraid if you ate something that was contaminated then you would become ill. So I stayed right with the American places. And one of the worst things in a jeep, I was behind in a jeep that had -- I was in the jeep, and in front of the jeep is what they called a honey bucket. It was an ox driven cart with human fertilizer. They used human fertilizer to fertilize their plants. They had beautiful strawberries and fruits and everything like that and they used that, and it would almost knock you out before you got through the tunnel, and I had a lot of weird experiences like that. And you had to get used to the Japanese. Sometimes when they said yes, they meant no. And of course, it was hard to get something from the States. So, I went to a dress maker, I got some brocade, I was going to a dance and I wanted to make -- I told them how I wanted it and everything. They took my measurements and everything, and smiled graciously. All through the interpreter. And I said I would come back for the fitting, and when I came back they didn't done anything, I said, "Well, you haven't done it. You haven't gotten the garment together at all." And they said, "Well, you were happy at the time weren't you?" "Yes, I was happy." "Well we made you happy. We didn't have any intentions of carry it out, until we got ready to make the garment for you." All through the interpreter. Many, many unusual circumstances and many, many trips over there. We went to the Mikimoto's Pearl Farm. He was the originator of the cultured pearl, and he imported the insert that you put in the oyster -- was from the Mississippi bottom, Mother of Pearl, and he would insert that in there, and then the nucleus would form around there, and they'd put it down in the ocean for a certain period of time. And then when we were there, the women that had greater lung power, they would dive down and bring those back and get the oysters up to them, and then they would put them on a tray. And we could pick out the oyster that we wanted, because we knew there would be a pearl in there, because it was all his pearl Farm there at Kobe Bay in Japan. And I had a beautiful pearl, and I gave it to my niece. I said, "When your sixteen I'll have this made into a ring for you, that would be when you're mature enough that the ring would fit." So I gave that to her, to my oldest niece.

sp.speaker: Olivia L. Olson
sp.p: Did you ever see General McArthur while you were there?

sp.speaker: Mary Cummings Jongeward
sp.p: No, I didn't. He had a private elevator, nobody was permitted in the elevator, but he was the only one who was permitted in there. Then he had -- he wanted a lot of to do over him, and whenever he left the building he always had a lot of people posted. You know, McArthur was not making his entrance out of his quarters there and going -- he always had the escort, motorcycles, and big escort whenever he would leave the building. He just thought that he was God, that nothing could touch him. And of course then -- Truman thought he had to be removed, he was getting too arrogant, too conceited. Of course he was actually a well known person at West Point, he'd been the higher upper class. He was born in Little Rock, Arkansas. He was outstanding General but, Truman brought him back and he retired, I mean, he died, I think in New York.

sp.speaker: Olivia L. Olson
sp.p: Can you tell me where you went after Japan?

sp.speaker: Mary Cummings Jongeward
sp.p: Well, I came back. Two years from over there, I mean, three years over there, I came back for my assignment, and the paper said ACLMACMD. Well I got to figure this out. Where am I going? Thirty day leave, and that must be Maryland. I'm going to some place in the State of Maryland. So I kept asking, showing the orders, nobody around there knew. They weren't military, they didn't know. I got on the train, and I asked different people along the way. Then when I got closer, after leaving Saint Louis, changed trains there, by going into Baltimore, I finally saw somebody. I said, "Can you tell me where in the world, I have a ticket to Baltimore." They said, "Oh, they should have put on there Edgewood Arsenal, you're going to Edgewood Arsenal." A very well known place, and it had changed the name to Army Chemical Center, because they were doing a lot of chemical work there. And so I got there in that Army Chemical Center and everybody always called it Edgewood Arsenal. And then from there I did a lot of paperwork, and it was a beautiful assignment, because I was a short distance from Baltimore. One hour to New York. I'd get -- on the weekends when I had time off, get on the train go into the Penn Station there in New York City, shop in the morning, see a play in the afternoon, opera in the evening, go back on the train, go back to Edgewood.

sp.speaker: Olivia L. Olson
sp.p: About what year was this?

sp.speaker: Mary Cummings Jongeward
sp.p: That was in the 50s.

sp.speaker: Olivia L. Olson
sp.p: Where did you go after your assignment?

sp.speaker: Mary Cummings Jongeward
sp.p: Then after that my mother was ill. I got a compassionate transfer back to -- my sister was living with -- my mother was living with my sister in Saint Angelo, Texas, and the nearest place was -- again, back to Fort Sam. So, I got transferred back there. And I would go on weekends when I had time off to help my sister, because she had quite a number of children and trying to take care of my mother, it was a hardship on her. So, I did what I could there, and then when I got back up there in the quarters I met -- that's where I met my husband, through a mutual friend, and we went together for two years. And then he had orders to go to Germany. And then we came back to Arkansas, back to Prairie Road, my hometown, where I was born, and where I was Baptized. And I wanted to be married in the same little town, came back there and got married, and then he was on orders to go to Germany. And then took a little while for me to get over there, but I managed. And he was supposed to go to Bremen, Germany and I was supposed to go to headquarters in Heidelberg, and they changed my orders so that we could be together.

sp.speaker: Olivia L. Olson
sp.p: Wonderful, about what year was that?

sp.speaker: Mary Cummings Jongeward
sp.p: And that was in '60, '61, 1961, and we were over there when Kennedy was assassinated, and they didn't know what to do with us. Whether ______ were armed ends or what to do. Anyway they didn't do anything, but I was there during that period, and we came back in 1964 from -- came back on the General Patch Ship and had -- we worked in security. I worked in the cage there handling classified information there in Germany. I had interesting experiences there in Germany. Many, many stories I can tell you. I don't want to elaborate so much but.

sp.speaker: Olivia L. Olson
sp.p: That's alright.

sp.speaker: Mary Cummings Jongeward
sp.p: Many, many things. One time they said your supposed to be creating German/American relationship, and they would take us in buses to a restaurant, and we'd be the only American couple speaking English, and then surrounded with maybe six or eight other couples at the table. And this one particular time they had Venaschnitzel. You know what that is? The veal cutlet. And so when they started playing the German, the real heavy music, my husband being the polite thing, he asked the woman to dance. And then the man looked at me, I had been eating the Venaschnitzel, and there was no silverware at all, but they had big huge linen napkins. And the music kept going on, and he kept looking at me and I thought, Well, what is this? He's not doing the polite thing by asking me to dance, and finally after I finished eating the Venaschnitzel, I put it down, I mean, put my hands down and wrapped it very carefully on the heavy linen napkin, and then he asked me to dance. He didn't want me putting greasy fingers on his clothes. That was it. So you know unusual things like that. And then we worked with the Germans in the offices where I had worked, and a German woman who had been -- her father realized the importance of her learning English, and so he sent her to Oxford, and she learned the pure English, and so I worked with her in the office in charge of the section there.

sp.speaker: Olivia L. Olson
sp.p: Was there someone that you admired or looked up to that was in the service with you that you would like to talk about?

sp.speaker: Mary Cummings Jongeward
sp.p: Well, I made different assignments, and where I was assigned -- and nobody in particularly like you would look up to an individual that just helped you get promoted, things like that. I didn't have anybody like that. I made things on my own.

sp.speaker: Olivia L. Olson
sp.p: What was the truth moral like when you were in the war?

sp.speaker: Mary Cummings Jongeward
sp.p: Well I thought it was very good. I was there when WAXA had their first anniversary and that was a memorable occasion when -- I was there in 1943 and their first anniversary was May of 1944 and they made a lot to do of it. And their Armed Forces Day, they made a big to do of that. And over in Germany, you know, since we were creating German/America relationship they thought that was wonderful, because I could get them some free ice cream. They loved our American ice cream.

sp.speaker: Olivia L. Olson
sp.p: Now, why did you choose to stay in the military once the war was over?

sp.speaker: Mary Cummings Jongeward
sp.p: Well, I had been in that long. They said I was over the hump, well over the hump. If you get ten years, you're over the hump, over ten years. I thought well, I'm going to continue on toward retirement, because I've gotten over -- in other words, I didn't want to waste ten years of my life, and I'll stay with it, and I'll put up with whatever happens. I'll put up with it, because at one time it was the duration plus, you couldn't have, and then you did have a choice. But I stayed with it, because I thought well this will be like my degree, this will be like my college degree. I'll stay with it, get my retirement from putting in at least 20 years, which I did. My husband and I both put in over 20 years.

sp.speaker: Olivia L. Olson
sp.p: What -- do you recall what your last days of the service were like?

sp.speaker: Mary Cummings Jongeward
sp.p: I was in Fort Dix, New Jersey and I was an instructor there and they were very short on instructors and they wanted me to stay on, but my husband was ready to retire. And he had said, "I've been through three wars, and I'm afraid I'm not going to make the next one baby, going to Vietnam." He says, "I'm afraid I'm not going to make another one. Let's retire. We have over 20 years." I said, "Well, that's all right with me." But he got released pretty quickly, but they kept hanging on and they were going to offer me the super ______ if I would stay on, and I said, "No, I'm not going to stay on with my husband out," I would just take my retirement too.

sp.speaker: Olivia L. Olson
sp.p: Good. Now, if you could advise young people today about going into the service, what would you say to them?

sp.speaker: Mary Cummings Jongeward
sp.p: Well you have to regiment yourself to be able to follow orders. You follow orders and then you question later. You don't question first. And you got used to that. You were regimented. You had to get used to the regular hours, your training periods and all that. And if you're not, if you just live the kind of a life that you can't put up with a lot of circumstances, then you don't have any business in there. Because you have to put up -- I had never -- I shouldn't say this, but I never been around colored people, you know, and you had to tolerate them, they would be over you in some section and they would be telling you what -- it was a little bit galling. I had to tolerate it, and I just accepted it and that was it.

sp.speaker: Olivia L. Olson
sp.p: Is there anything you would like to add that we haven't discussed that would help future history students understand about your position in the service?

sp.speaker: Mary Cummings Jongeward
sp.p: Well I'd say they offer a lot of incentive now to reenlist, and the pay is very good. It's much more than in a civilian life, if they stick with it. But if their just on just short term, just a three year, it's not much to their advantage, because that's just a temporary thing. I talk with different people, if they stay with it, you can tolerate it. You get use to it, you can tolerate it.

sp.speaker: Olivia L. Olson
sp.p: Well I want to thank you, Mary, for your wonderful interview, and we want to close now, and unless there's something else that you would like to say?

sp.speaker: Mary Cummings Jongeward
sp.p: No. There's so many other things, you know. There just immaterial things that happened while I was in there, you know, interesting experiences, and of course after I got out. Cause your not interested in that. We went to the Women's Memorial.

sp.speaker: Olivia L. Olson
sp.p: Wonderful.

sp.speaker: Mary Cummings Jongeward
sp.p: In 1997. And my nieces -- I had, we four sisters and four nieces went with us. We stayed there at the hotel in Washington, DC.

sp.speaker: Olivia L. Olson
sp.p: How nice.

sp.speaker: Mary Cummings Jongeward
sp.p: Madison Hotel.

sp.speaker: Olivia L. Olson
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Mary Cummings Jongeward
sp.p: And we went to the memorial for the women's service and that was a wonderful occasion, and my nephew came down from New York and escorted me. We had our formals on, and he came down and was my escort for me at the formal gatherings and the dinners and things. And that was a very special occasion. And I appreciated my sisters going with me, because it was quite costly, you know, it was well over a thousand dollars or more to make the trip and back, and I appreciated that. They said, "You've been giving gifts to our children, and we want to do something for you."

sp.speaker: Olivia L. Olson
sp.p: How nice.

sp.speaker: Mary Cummings Jongeward
sp.p: And of course I never had any children, and we tried to adopt over there, but it didn't work out, and so we never adopted and so I never had children.

sp.speaker: Olivia L. Olson
sp.p: Well this concludes our interview, but I want to thank you very much.

sp.speaker: Mary Cummings Jongeward
sp.p: Well yes, it's been real nice talking to you, and I hope I haven't extended myself too much.

sp.speaker: Olivia L. Olson
sp.p: Oh, you haven't.
